Why recipes round the numbers

Exact conversions give awkward numbers: 350 °F is 176.7 °C. Recipe writers round to the nearest 10 °C, so 350 °F becomes 180 °C and 180 °C becomes 350 °F. The 3-degree difference is far smaller than the error in most home ovens, which can run 10–25 degrees hot or cold. An oven thermometer that hangs from the rack is the cheapest way to find out what yours actually does.

Fan and convection ovens

A fan oven blows hot air around the food, so it cooks faster and more evenly at the same setting. Most UK and European recipes list both temperatures; American recipes usually assume a conventional oven. The usual rule is to set a fan oven about 25 °F or 20 °C lower, or keep the temperature and start checking 5–10 minutes early.

Gas marks

Gas marks come from British gas cookers and still appear in older UK recipes. Mark 4 is the classic baking temperature, 350 °F or 180 °C. Each mark above 1 adds about 25 °F, and the lowest settings are ¼ and ½.

Questions

What is 350 °F in Celsius?

350 °F is 176.7 °C, which recipes round to 180 °C. It’s gas mark 4, or about 160 °C in a fan oven.

What is 180 °C in Fahrenheit?

180 °C is 356 °F. Recipes treat it as 350 °F, the standard baking temperature.

How do I convert a recipe for a fan oven?

Lower the temperature by about 20 °C (25 °F), or keep it the same and check for doneness 5 to 10 minutes early.

What temperature is gas mark 6?

Gas mark 6 is 400 °F or 200 °C, a hot oven used for roasting vegetables and baking bread rolls.
